title: A geometry figure is a render of a shape, so the evidence of correctness is the number printed beside it, not the picture
summary: Three engines draw the same revolved nozzle, and four feature figures show revolve, fillet, shell and sweep on a signed-distance kernel. Renders of different correct kernels look alike, so read what each render is supposed to show, check it against the construction, and rely on printed volumes and watertightness for agreement.

media.alt: A 3D surface render, titled sdf: revolved_nozzle, of a rotationally symmetric nozzle lying along the x axis from 0 to about 0.065 metres: a wide cylinder of radius about 0.02 metres, a conical taper, then a narrower cylinder of about 0.01 metres radius. The surface is light blue with a visible triangle mesh.

source.caption: SDF-kernel revolved nozzle
group: 36_sdf_smooth_blend: SDF kernel, smooth blend of two spheres
source.note: Eight cfdcore geometry-kernel renders: three engines on one nozzle, plus feature renders from a signed-distance-field kernel. The project caption for 14 states an enclosed volume of 5.4633e-05 shared by all three engines; that number is not visible in any image.

read_the_figure.question: Does the generated surface have the shape the construction should give, and do independent engines agree on it?
read_the_figure.axes: Nozzle renders: x, y, z in metres, with x the axis of revolution (0 to 0.07 m) and y, z the cross-section (about -0.02 to 0.02 m). Feature renders: unlabelled units, axes about -2 to 2 or -1.5 to 1.5; the title gives the feature and its arguments.
look_at: The profile along the axis: a wide cylinder, a taper, a narrow cylinder, which is the outline that was revolved.
The cross-section is circular everywhere (a revolved shape): rings of triangles around the axis.
The triangle density: a mesh fine enough that the taper edges look sharp and the cylinders look round.
Axis scales: unequal scaling squeezes shapes. The fillet render, for example, shows two ellipsoids, not spheres, because the axes are scaled differently.
In the feature renders, whether the feature in the title is visible: a hole for the annulus, a rounded transition for the fillet, a hollow for the shell, a ring for the torus.
read_the_figure.proves: A render shows only that something plausible was meshed. Cross-engine agreement is established by printed quantities (enclosed volume, watertight check, bounding box), as the project caption for the third engine reports. Three images that look identical show that no gross difference exists, not that the surfaces agree to within tolerance.
if_wrong: A nozzle whose taper ends are rounded or whose radius changes between engines: the profile was sampled differently, or the isosurface resolution is coarse.
A surface with holes or isolated fragments: not watertight, so volume and boundary-condition tagging will fail.
Unequal axis scales: misleading shape, not a geometry error, but it can hide one.
A feature that does not appear (a fillet between spheres drawn as two separate bodies, a shell drawn opaque from outside): the render does not demonstrate the feature.
must_check: Equal aspect axes, so that spheres look spherical and circles look circular.
The same view angle and scale across engines being compared.
Printed volume, area, watertightness and tolerance, not just pictures.
For features such as shell: a cut-away or a section, otherwise the hollow cannot be seen.
Units on the axes (here the nozzle is in metres; the feature renders are unitless).
as_drawn: The three nozzle renders (SDF, Gmsh, PicoGK) look the same at this view, with the same axes, profile and mesh pattern. The images do not carry the volume; the project's caption states 5.4633e-05 in each engine.

A profile read off the axes: radius about 0.02 m for the first third, a taper to about 0.01 m, and a narrow section reaching x of about 0.065 m. An approximate volume from these numbers is about 5.5e-05 cubic metres.
Fillet render: two ellipsoids side by side and separate, with different axis scales; a blend between the two is not visible in this view.
Shell render: a closed opaque sphere, titled t = 0.3; the hollow interior is not visible from outside.
Torus (circular sweep): a ring with a clear central hole, vertical extent about -0.5 to 0.5 on axes that reach 2.
Smooth blend of two spheres: one peanut-shaped surface with a smooth neck on a fine triangle mesh.

terms.meaning: A function d(x) that gives the distance to the surface, negative inside and positive outside. The surface is its zero set.
Sweep a planar profile around an axis. For an SDF the 3D distance is the 2D profile's distance evaluated at the radius and axial position.
A blend of two SDFs that replaces the sharp minimum by a rounded one, giving a fillet-like neck.
Hollow out a solid to a wall thickness t by taking the absolute value of its SDF and offsetting.
Move a profile along a path; a disc swept around a circle gives a torus.
A closed triangle mesh with no gaps, so that enclosed volume and inside-outside tests are well defined.
Extracting the triangle surface where the SDF crosses zero on a grid; its resolution limits the sharpness of edges.

remember: Renders of correct and slightly wrong surfaces can look identical; compare numbers.
Volume of a revolved profile is 2 pi times the centroid radius times the profile area (Pappus).
Equal aspect axes are part of an honest 3D render.
A smooth union rounds the neck between two bodies; a plain union leaves a crease.
A shell cannot be judged from the outside.

understand.title: Cross-engine agreement
understand.text: Three independent engines build the same shape from the same profile. The picture proves little because one nozzle meshed three ways looks the same. The checks that matter are numeric: equal enclosed volume to many digits, watertightness, and equal boundary tags.

understand.title: Features on an SDF kernel
understand.text: Because a shape is a distance field, features are algebra on fields: revolve is a change of coordinates, shell is an offset of |d|, a fillet is a smooth minimum, and a sweep of a disc around a circle is the torus distance. This is why the same kernel can produce both the tidy annulus and the peanut.

understand.title: What each feature figure should show
understand.text: Revolve of a rectangle gives a ring with a hole; a shell of a sphere gives a hollow with thin wall; a smooth blend of two spheres gives a single body with a neck. If the render shows something else (two separate bodies, a solid sphere) it is not yet a demonstration of the feature.

steps.title: A sphere as an SDF
steps.note: Negative inside, zero on the surface, positive outside.

steps.title: Union and its smooth version
steps.note: The polynomial smooth minimum: it equals the minimum when the two distances differ by more than k and rounds the crease inside a band of width k. A larger k gives a thicker neck, as in the peanut render.

steps.title: Revolve
steps.note: A planar profile's distance field is evaluated at radius and axial position. A rectangle away from the axis gives an annulus; the nozzle profile gives the nozzle.

steps.title: Shell
steps.note: The set where |d| is less than t/2 is a layer of thickness t around the original surface; with t = 0.3 on a unit sphere the wall is thin and the inside is hollow.

steps.title: Circular sweep to a torus
steps.note: A disc of radius r swept around a circle of radius R in the xy plane.

steps.title: Volume of a revolved profile (Pappus)
steps.note: For a nozzle built of cylinders and a cone, the volume is the sum of cylinder volumes pi R squared L and the frustum volume pi L / 3 times (R1 squared + R1 R2 + R2 squared).

worked.title: Volume of the nozzle from read-off dimensions
worked.problem: Read from the axes (approximate): a cylinder of radius 0.02 m and length 0.03 m, a cone from radius 0.02 to 0.01 m over 0.015 m, and a cylinder of radius 0.01 m and length 0.02 m. Estimate the enclosed volume and compare with the caption's 5.4633e-05.
worked.answer: About 5.5e-05 cubic metres, which agrees with 5.4633e-05 to within the accuracy of the read-off lengths (the dimensions are estimated by eye, so this is a consistency check, not a verification).

analyze.q: Three engines produce renders that cannot be told apart by eye. What three numbers would you compare to say they agree?
analyze.hint: Volume, surface area, bounding box, watertightness.

analyze.q: The fillet render shows two separate bodies. List two reasons, one about the construction and one about the view.
analyze.hint: A blend radius too small for the gap; a non-equal aspect or the camera.

analyze.q: A shell of thickness t = 0.3 on a unit-radius sphere: what is the inner radius if the shell is centred on the original surface, and what is it if the shell is grown inward?

evaluate.q: Is a figure of three identical renders adequate as evidence of cross-engine agreement in a portfolio? What would you add?
evaluate.hint: The printed volume table and tolerances.

evaluate.q: Which of the feature renders would you replace first with a better view?
evaluate.hint: Features that cannot be seen from outside.

create: Make a cut-away render of the shell and a section view of the fillet neck, with equal aspect axes and a printed wall thickness.
Design a table for the three engines: volume, surface area, bounding box, watertightness, number of triangles, and the relative differences.

checks.q: Why is agreement of volumes more convincing than agreement of pictures?
checks.answer: A volume to five digits detects differences far smaller than an eye can see in a render, and it integrates over the whole surface.

checks.q: A cylinder of radius 0.01 m and length 0.02 m: what is its volume?
checks.answer: pi times 1e-4 times 0.02, about 6.3e-06 cubic metres.

checks.q: Why does revolving a profile that crosses the axis give a self-intersection problem?
checks.answer: Points on the other side of the axis map to the same radii as points on this side, so the profile overlaps its mirror image and the solid is not well defined; profiles must stay on one side of the axis.

checks.q: A torus render with a visible hole and fine mesh. Does it validate the sweep?
checks.answer: Only qualitatively. Compare the computed volume with 2 pi squared R r squared and the surface area with 4 pi squared R r.

checks.q: How would you demonstrate a shell on a sphere in one picture?
checks.answer: Cut the mesh with a plane through the centre and show the cross-section ring with its thickness dimensioned.
